text: The University of Puerto Rico (Spanish: Universidad de Puerto Rico; often shortened to UPR) is the main public university system in the U.S. Commonwealth of Puerto Rico and operates as a government-owned corporation with 11 campuses, approximately 44,200 students, and approximately 4,450 faculty members. It offers the largest and most diverse academic programs in the commonwealth, including 472 academic programs, of which 32 lead to a doctorate. In 1900, the Escuela Normal Industrial was established in Fajardo as the first higher education center in Puerto Rico, with an initial enrollment of 20 students and 5 professors; the following year, it moved to Río Piedras. On March 12, 1903, the legislature authorized the founding of the University of Puerto Rico, and that day the "Escuela Normal" was proclaimed as its first department. As new schools were built to resemble those in the United States, UPR became the primary institution for training teachers proficient in English to support the Americanization project. In 1908, the Morrill-Nelson Act was extended to Puerto Rico, designating the university a "Land Grant College" that allows the use of federal land for agriculture, science, and engineering. In 1910, the College of Liberal Arts was established, and in 1911, the College of Agriculture at Mayagüez was founded; in 1912, it was renamed the College of Agriculture and Mechanic Arts. In 1913, the Departments of Pharmacy and Law were established. Following the University Act of 1923, UPR reorganized administratively, becoming independent from the Insular Department of Education, with the Board of Trustees as its governing body and the Rector as its principal officer. In 1923, Lidio Cruz Monclova began offering Puerto Rican history and literature courses; upon arriving from the RUM, Rafael W. Ramírez de Arellano began teaching those courses at Río Piedras. In 1924, UPR became administratively independent from the Department of Public Instruction, and the governor appointed the first Rector. In 1925, a Spanish Department was created and assigned to the Summer School to teach foreign professors the language. In 1926, the School of Commerce (later School of Business Administration) and the School of Tropical Medicine were established. In 1927, then Rector Thomas E. Benner established the Department of Hispanic Studies, led by Federico de Onís; the Revista de Estudios Hispánicos began publication the following year, with professors including Antonio S. Pedreira, Ángel del Río, Concha Meléndez, Tomás Navarro Tomás, and Margot Arce de Vázquez; that year, the Master of Arts in Hispanic Studies became the institution's first graduate program. In 1928, the San Felipe Segundo hurricane struck Puerto Rico, causing serious damage to the Río Piedras campus, prompting staff and faculty to begin a reconstruction effort. In 1929, a Department of History and Social Sciences was created within the College of Arts and Sciences, directed by Pilar Barbosa de Rosario. In 1932, Rector Carlos Chardón organized a Committee of Publications; he supported the development of archaeologists and pushed Arturo Morales Carrión to study anthropology abroad, though the student declined. That year, the Alfa Fi Sigma fraternity was founded by students opposed to initiation rituals in other fraternities. In 1933, several students joined strikes in the tobacco and needlework industries. In 1935, the U.S. Congress extended to Puerto Rico the benefits of the Bankhead-Jones Act, providing funding for research and building more facilities. During the following years, major structures in Spanish Renaissance style were constructed in the Río Piedras quadrangle, including the Tower Theatre. In 1938, Augusto Rodríguez composed the music and lyrics for Arriví Francisco's Alma Mater, the university anthem. Pedreira succeeded Onís as director of the Revista de Estudios Hispánicos and remained until 1939. By that year, UPR had increased its student enrollment to 5,000. Under Rector Juan B. Soto, most department directors were foreign, and the institution was part of the Americanization effort, with most classes taught in English; some local professors who supported the administration also taught in English. The emergence of a Puerto Rican academic nucleus led to internal conflicts reflecting broader political tensions. In 1940, Margot Arce de Vázquez and Jaime Benítez participated in a debate, with Arce de Vázquez advocating for more research, publications, exchanges, and a rigorous path to professorship, and Benítez opposing nationalism and favoring a European cultural sphere. Between 1941 and 1942, Pedro Muñoz Amaro and Isidro Díaz López led the student council, with Ricardo Alegría as secretary and Marcos A. Ramírez and Quiñones Elías as members. Act No. 135 of May 7, 1942, amended the university's structure by creating the Higher Education Council as its governing board and regulator of higher education in Puerto Rico; under this model, the UPR Rector selected a vicerector for the RUM and a board. That same year, Benítez was named Rector. The Tugwell Affair led to the formation of the Agrupación Reformista Universitaria by his supporters; in response, Marcos A. Ramírez left the student council in protest. In 1943, UPR's editorial was formally established under a board. Publications such as Ámbito criticized the university for failing to develop a "nativist intellectualism," while the gossip magazine El Cuko (authored by José Luis Torregrosa and Germán Rieckhoff Sampayo) adopted a socialist approach and made demands to the administration; another publication was the newspaper La Torre. In 1947, the university received accreditation from the Middle States Association of Colleges and Schools. In 1947, Antonio J. Colorado became director of the editorial. In 1953, a magazine named La Torre (not related to the newspaper) began publication. In 1954, then-professor Alegría protested before the Consejo de Educación Superior, arguing that visiting professors were given better privileges than local professors, believing Benítez's request for maximum salaries did not properly reflect competency. Vicente Geigel Polanco, who taught law and social sciences, was a proponent of reform and wrote essays on the subject, including La reforma universitaria and El problema educativo. Act No. 1 of 1966 restructured the university into three campuses—Río Piedras, Mayagüez, and Medical Sciences—resulting in Benítez ceasing to serve as Rector and becoming president, holding the office until 1971. The following year, regional colleges were established: Arecibo, Cayey, and Humacao; five more were created in subsequent years: Ponce (1969), Bayamón (1971), Aguadilla (1972), Carolina (1973), and Utuado (1978). In 1979, WRTU began broadcasting from the Río Piedras campus. Act No. 186 of August 7, 1998, provided for the gradual autonomy of regional schools under the Board of Trustees, leading to eleven autonomous units. In 2010–2011, a series of strikes occurred due to administrative budget cuts and an attempt to impose an $800 student quota. On July 2010, the Middle States Commission on Higher Education placed UPR's accreditation on probation due to governance concerns; by the end of 2011, all 11 campuses had regained full accreditation after demonstrating significant progress. In 2017, UPR staff organized a strike against budget cuts proposed by the Financial Oversight and Management Board for Puerto Rico. After Hurricane Maria, the university suffered damages totaling over $175 million, still facing structural damage months later and relying on FEMA funding for repairs; the hurricane also affected accreditation, as eight campuses were in non-compliance with the Middle States Commission on Higher Education. The eleven campuses reopened within two months of the hurricane, providing structure and normalcy. In 2019, during Jorge Haddock's tenure, the university newspaper Diálogo, after 32 years in print, was moved online and employees were laid off until only the editor and an assistant remained; they were reassigned, and the newspaper was moved from central administration to the Arecibo campus. In 2021, the Financial Oversight and Management Board cut $94 million from the UPR budget, which would have severely impacted operations; the local government intervened and assigned the necessary funds before the August semester began. The Board of Trustees is the governing body of the University of Puerto Rico. On April 30, 2013, Governor Alejandro García Padilla signed into law Act 13 of 2014, enacted by the 17th Legislative Assembly, which replaced the incumbent board with a new one; in 2017, the board was changed again by Governor Ricardo Rosselló. The campus radio station, WRTU Radio Universidad de Puerto Rico, was established in 1980 and is a public radio station with diverse musical and news programming, broadcasting both in FM and online. UPR has the highest selectivity index among all colleges and universities in Puerto Rico and has maintained a systemwide admission rate of 67% since 1997; its enrollment rate has surpassed 90% in the past five academic years. Tuition costs are $157 per undergraduate credit and $300 per graduate credit; in 2017, undergraduate credit cost was $53 and graduate credit cost was $172; the undergraduate credit cost is expected to rise to $177 by 2027. In recent years, student enrollment has declined: during the 2009–2010 academic year, 52,791 students were enrolled; by 2014–2015, this number dropped to 47,314; in 2022–2023, enrollment was 44,233 across the 11 campuses. The university is classified as "R2: Doctoral Universities – High research activity." On October 15, 2010, UPR received over $25 million from the National Science Foundation (NSF) to support research in nanotechnology, through the Puerto Rico EPSCoR program, which has received over $180 million from NSF, NASA, the U.S. Department of Energy, and the U.S. Department of Defense since its creation 24 years ago. On August 24, 2020, the university announced ten investigations to prevent and mitigate the spread of COVID-19 as part of $1.7 million received from the local government. According to the QS World University Rankings 2022 (published in 2021), UPR ranks 40th in Latin America, down from 37 in 2020, but still above previous rankings of 42 in 2018 and 62 in 2015; as a system, it placed in the 800–1000 bracket in the 2018 QS World University Rankings and in the 801–1000 bracket in the Times Higher Education rankings. UPR was ranked among the best 20 universities in Latin America by SCImago in 2010; it ranked 18th overall and the University of Puerto Rico at Mayagüez ranked 78th by Webometrics in Latin America; UPR is the number one university in the Caribbean according to Webometrics. The system's only school of engineering at the Mayagüez campus is accredited by ABET and graduates more than 600 engineers per year, and it was named the top engineering school for Hispanics by Hispanic Engineer & Information Technology Magazine. In 2020, Dr. Gerardo Moller, director of NASA's grant consortium in Puerto Rico, stated that 25% of Hispanic employees hired by NASA are UPR graduates. Research activity, measured by external funding, has grown exponentially since 1985, doubling every five years; in 2007–2008, UPR received over $87 million for research.
